title: Algorithms to Live By (Christian & Griffiths) — Applied
description: Self-study deck on 'Algorithms to Live By': optimal stopping, explore/exploit, caching, scheduling, Bayes, overfitting, and backoff — computer science as life advice.

questions.prompt: In optimal stopping (the 'secretary problem'), the look-then-leap rule says: observe and reject roughly what fraction, then take the next candidate better than all seen so far?
questions.explanation: 1/e ≈ 37% — spend the first 37% calibrating, then commit to the next record-beater.

questions.prompt: The explore/exploit trade-off is formalized in computer science as the ___ problem.
questions.explanation: Multi-armed bandits model when to try new options (explore) vs stick with the best known (exploit).

questions.prompt: According to the book, how much you should explore versus exploit depends most on:

options: How much time or how many tries remain
The size of the dataset only

questions.explanation: Explore more when much future remains; exploit as the interval shrinks — 'be optimistic when young.'

questions.prompt: The caching eviction policy that discards the least-recently-used item is abbreviated ___.
questions.explanation: LRU approximates the unbeatable-but-clairvoyant 'evict what we'll need furthest in the future.'

questions.prompt: To minimize the MAXIMUM lateness across a set of tasks with due dates, schedule them by:
questions.explanation: Earliest Due Date minimizes the maximum lateness — handle whatever is due soonest first.

questions.prompt: To minimize the SUM of completion times (clear the most tasks soonest), schedule by:
questions.explanation: Shortest Processing Time first minimizes total/average completion time — weight by importance/time for a priority version.

questions.prompt: Under Bayes's rule, when you have very little data your prior assumptions dominate the estimate.
questions.explanation: Sparse evidence leans on the prior; data progressively overrides it as it accumulates.

questions.prompt: The book's antidote to overfitting is to:

options: Favor simpler models and stop training earlier
Add as many parameters as possible
Always fit the training data exactly

questions.explanation: Penalize complexity and use early stopping; fitting noise generalizes worse than a simpler model.

questions.prompt: When a shared network is congested, the proven strategy of waiting random, doubling intervals before retrying is called exponential ___.
questions.explanation: Exponential backoff spaces retries to relieve congestion instead of worsening it.

questions.prompt: Apply explore/exploit to a concrete decision in your life (where to eat, which projects to take). Explain why the right balance shifts as your remaining time horizon changes.

payload.rubric: Picks a real decision; argues explore-heavy early (long horizon, info has time to pay off) and exploit-heavy late; bonus for naming regret/UCB-style 'optimism.'
